title: Shut Out at the Oscars of Food: Indian-American Finalists Go Home Empty-Handed at 2026 James Beard Awards
excerpt: A record slate of Indian restaurateurs and chefs reached the 2026 finals, but none claimed a medal in Chicago — even as immigrant stories dominated the night.
body:
The James Beard Awards — the ceremony the food world only half-jokingly calls its Oscars — were handed out Monday night at Chicago's Lyric Opera, and for the swelling ranks of Indian-American restaurateurs and chefs who had fought their way to the finals, the evening ended in polite applause rather than acceptance speeches. A record diaspora presence on the 2026 ballot translated, when the envelopes were opened, into zero medals.

For a community that has spent two decades arguing that Indian food deserves a seat at America's fine-dining table, it was a night of being seen but not yet crowned.

## Context & Background

The disappointment stings precisely because the build-up was so promising. Srijith Gopinathan and Ayesha Thapar — the husband-and-wife team behind the Cal-India Collective, whose Ettan, Copra, Eylan and Little Blue Door have redefined upscale Indian cooking across the San Francisco Peninsula — were finalists for Outstanding Restaurateur, one of the night's marquee national prizes. In Washington, Suresh Sundas of Tapori was the lone non-Pennsylvania chef nominated for Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic. And in Las Vegas, the reborn Tamba, a modern Indian spot whose name means "copper" in Hindi, was a Best New Restaurant finalist in one of the most competitive categories in the entire awards.

These were not token nominations. The James Beard Foundation, now marking its 40th anniversary, frames its prizes as both recognition and prophecy — past honorees include Alice Waters, Wolfgang Puck and Emeril Lagasse, all of whom rode the so-called "Beard bump" to household-name status.

## Current Developments

When the winners were read out, however, the trophies went elsewhere. Outstanding Restaurateur was won by Dana Street of Portland, Maine. Best New Restaurant went to Lei, a 28-seat Chinatown wine bar in New York rooted in Chinese home cooking. Best Chef: Mid-Atlantic was claimed by Jesse Ito of Royal Sushi & Izakaya in Philadelphia. Michael Tusk of San Francisco's Quince took Outstanding Chef, and Philadelphia's southern Thai restaurant Kalaya was named Outstanding Restaurant.

If Indian cuisine did not win, immigration itself was unmistakably the theme of the night. Emerging Chef winner Adrian Torres of Maximo in Texas, the son of Mexican immigrants and a DACA recipient, told the room that for too long "fear was our story." Illinois Governor JB Pritzker, addressing the crowd of roughly 2,000, said restaurant-industry immigrants had been "under siege." For diaspora diners watching, the subtext was familiar even if the medal was not.

## Diaspora Impact

For NRIs, the Beard Awards have become a kind of cultural barometer — a way of measuring whether the food of home is treated as serious cuisine or exotic novelty. The fact that Indian names now populate finalist lists in California, the Mid-Atlantic and the Southwest is itself the story of a generation: the children of restaurateurs who once served chicken tikka masala to skeptical American palates are now plating wood-fired Cal-Indian tasting menus that land on the Michelin Guide.

Gopinathan and Thapar had captured that ambition in their nomination statement, describing a cuisine "that feels bright, vibrant, and rooted in California." That vision did not win a medallion this year, but the trajectory — from semifinalist whispers to repeat finalists — suggests the wait may be measured in seasons, not decades.

## What's Next

The optimistic reading among diaspora food watchers is that finalist density precedes victory. Indian restaurateurs were semifinalists, then finalists; the next logical step is the podium. Chai Pani's Meherwan and Molly Irani — also Outstanding Restaurateur finalists this year — already proved the ceiling can be broken, having won Outstanding Restaurant in 2022 for their Asheville flagship.

With Sundas, the Cal-India team, and Tamba's Dhillon family all likely to remain in contention, and a still-deepening bench of modern Indian kitchens from Manhattan to Houston, the question is no longer whether an Indian restaurant belongs in the conversation. It is simply when one will finally hear its name called.
